newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries in tight ranges ahead of retail data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries in tight ranges ahead of retail data.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities closed in tight ranges again on Wednesday as traders awaited comprehensive news on the state of the U.S. economy on Thursday.
Market participants were reluctant to stake major positions ahead of the release of May retail sales data on Thursday and prices remained in narrow ranges.
Analysts polled by Reuters expected, on average, that retail sales would rise 0.4 percent in May after a 0.3 percent decline in April.
Helping keep a lid on prices was weakness in the dollar as it continued a slide that has seen it slip more than 13 percent against the yen in the last six weeks.

"The bond market has taken a sort of new lease on life with the latest employment numbers -- mainly on the wage side," said David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co. He noted that average hourly earnings rose only about four cents an hour in May, leading to the view that wage inflation remains contained in the current tight labor market.
The prospect of no near-term inflation was pushing the stock market to new highs, Jones said.
"The real issue is: 'Was the slowing seen in second quarter just a pause or real?' My own view is it was just a pause," said Jones.

Whether the Federal Reserve will keep policy unchanged or move again to tighten monetary policy is an issue for market participants, Jones said, but most now seem to be hedging their bets the Fed will stay on the sidelines during its next Federal Open Market Committee meeting in July.
The economy is now catching another breath as the long expansion continues, Jones said.
He said current consumption and business expansion rates are at the best levels since the early 1960s.
"We're waiting for more data. The next two days will be important," said Mark Vitner, economist with the capital markets group at First Union Corp.
Producer prices, business inventories and the University of Michigan survey were due on Friday.
Vitner said the Fed may need more evidence of a slowing economy before deciding to remain on the sidelines.

Vitner said the Fed may only tighten short-term interest rates by another 75 basis points between now and the spring of 1998. The unemployment rate could drop to as low as 4.5 percent without raising hackles at the Fed, he said.
Vitner said wage gains could occur, but should not present a major problem given the current economic scenario.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has made clear the central bank would strike preemptively to control inflation should the economy continue to grow at a strong pace -- even without stronger inflation statistics.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended at 97-14/32, up 6/32, yielding 6.83 percent.

Two-year notes ended at 100-5/32, unchanged to yield 6.16 percent. Five-year notes rose 1/32 to 100-7/32 to yield 6.45 percent and the 10-year note was up 3/32 to 100-16/32, its yield at 6.56 percent.
Three-month bill rates fell five basis points to 4.85 percent, six-month rates were down one basis point at 5.19 percent and year bill rates were unchanged at 5.43 percent.
